rationale: A wins because it knows where the floor is: “Airtable's agents can now update your records and draft your emails. It has not said how often they get it wrong” turns a disclosed absence into a legitimate enterprise-IT story. B has good bones, but it starts decorating gaps with “employees are the ones left to catch what they get wrong” and a “prevailing belief” the update did not supply. That is how a usable angle becomes a reporter's first fact-check failure.
gaps_in_A: “publicly abandoning that identity” slightly overstates the update. The facts say Airtable is shifting messaging, not that it has publicly disowned the old category.

The valuation angle is honest but soft: “what the company is worth today” needs a current mark, secondary transaction, investor, or filing. The set flags that gap, but the angle cannot move without it.
The category angle still needs the missing customer proof it asks for: “one enterprise team, named.” Without that, it is a company-positioning story, not a market-shift story.
gaps_in_B: “employees are the ones left to catch what they get wrong” invents an operational burden. The update says agents update statuses or draft emails; it does not say employees catch errors.
“the prevailing belief... that enterprise AI agents are now trustworthy enough to act autonomously on production data” is manufactured context. No prevailing belief or market evidence was supplied.
“send communications” overreaches from “drafting emails.” Drafting is not sending, and that distinction matters in an agent-risk story.
The fourth angle is padding in nicer clothes. “workplace-culture reporter” is a different desk, but the story is still the same undisclosed-reliability gap as angle three.
